1. Core Clinical Tension: A patient undergoing prolonged outpatient therapy and percutaneous drainage for a large resolving hepatic abscess develops new peripheral eosinophilia, paresthesias, and a rash. The core tension lies in distinguishing between medication-induced side effects (neurotoxicity and hypersensitivity from metronidazole) versus refractory or secondary infection requiring changes in drainage or antimicrobial therapy.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint occurs during outpatient clinical follow-up as the patient presents with new neurologic and dermatologic symptoms during treatment with an in-dwelling percutaneous drainage catheter, prior to formal assessment of fluoroscopic cavity resolution, completion of prolonged metronidazole therapy, and initiation of luminal cysticidal therapy.
3. Differential Distinctions: Refractory infection or secondary catheter-related bacterial superinfection was suspected due to slow volume reduction and new systemic signs (eosinophilia, rash), but regular fluoroscopic checks demonstrated steady abscess collapse. Metronidazole toxicity accounted for the paresthesias and hypersensitivity. The diagnosis of resolving invasive amebiasis with subsequent eradication of intestinal carriage was completed using luminal paromomycin.
case_prompt: A male patient with a large hepatic abscess managed with a percutaneous drainage catheter and targeted outpatient medical therapy presented for follow-up evaluation. During outpatient management, he reported new onset of paresthesias and a mild dermatologic rash, accompanied by newly documented peripheral eosinophilia. The hepatic collection exhibited a slow reduction in size and drainage output, requiring ongoing interventional radiology and clinical monitoring.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to the large size of the collection, slow drainage reduction, and new eosinophilia and cutaneous findings, but outpatient fluoroscopic cavity examinations demonstrated consistent progressive decrease in cavity size.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Additionally, he had regular outpatient fluoroscopic drain checks with IR, which showed a gradual decrease in the abscess size (see Figure 4).

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Adverse drug reaction (metronidazole neurotoxicity and hypersensitivity)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Paresthesias, rash, and eosinophilia were recognized as drug-related adverse effects of ongoing therapy; after careful discussion, therapy was maintained under close observation to ensure complete resolution of the large collection.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: In the outpatient setting, the patient continued metronidazole therapy (750 mg PO three times per day) but then developed eosinophilia, paresthesias, and a mild rash while on treatment. Given the size of his abscess and the slow reduction in abscess size and drain output, the decision was made to continue metronidazole until complete resolution of the abscess (16 weeks total). He made an informed decision to complete his course of metronidazole for his E. histolytica while his symptoms were closely monitored.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Complete radiological resolution of the amebic hepatic abscess after 16 weeks of metronidazole and drainage, followed by a targeted course of paromomycin to eradicate intraluminal Entamoeba histolytica cysts.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: He also completed a course of paromomycin (750 mg PO TID for 7 days) to eradicate intraluminal cysts after metronidazole was stopped at the end of Week 16. The drain was removed after the abscess had resolved after 16 weeks of metronidazole and effective drainage.
